claim: klf2a and klf2b are collectively orthologous to mammalian Klf2 in zebrafish
source: Zebrafish klf2a and klf2b are known to be collectively orthologous to mammalian Klf2 (Oates et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oates et al., 2001

claim: Endothelial klf2a expression is flow-dependent
source: Endothelial klf2a expression has been shown to be flow-dependent (Parmar et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Parmar et al., 2006

claim: klf2a knockdown by antisense morpholinos causes pericardial edema
source: its knockdown by antisense morpholinos was reported to cause pericardial edema, dysfunctional cardiac valves (Vermot et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Vermot et al., 2009

claim: klf2a knockdown by antisense morpholinos causes dysfunctional cardiac valves
source: its knockdown by antisense morpholinos was reported to cause pericardial edema, dysfunctional cardiac valves (Vermot et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Vermot et al., 2009

claim: klf2a knockdown by antisense morpholinos causes defective haematopoietic stem cell development
source: its knockdown by antisense morpholinos was reported to cause pericardial edema, dysfunctional cardiac valves (Vermot et al., 2009) and defective haematopoietic stem cell development (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011

claim: klf2ash317 mutant embryos do not exhibit obvious morphological phenotypes
source: However, unlike the aforementioned klf2a morpholino-induced cardiovascular defects, no obvious morphological phenotypes were observed in klf2ash317 mutant embryos (Novodvorsky et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Novodvorsky et al., 2015

claim: The predicted truncated Klf2a bns11 protein lacks the transrepression and zinc finger domains
source: Notably, the predicted truncated Klf2a bns11 protein lacks the transrepression and zinc finger domains (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by schematic representation in Figure 1A showing protein domains

claim: The predicted Klf2b bns12 protein contains only part of the transactivation domain
source: and the predicted Klf2b bns12 protein contains only part of the transactivation domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by schematic representation in Figure 1B showing protein domains

claim: Neither klf2abns11 nor klf2bbns12 mutants exhibit gross morphological defects
source: Surprisingly, unlike the klf2a morphants which have been reported to exhibit pericardial edema and cardiac defects (Vermot et al., 2009), neither klf2abns11 nor klf2bbns12 mutants exhibit gross morphological defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by brightfield images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C and citation to Vermot et al., 2009

claim: klf2a and klf2b single mutants can survive to become fertile adults
source: Close examination revealed no obvious cardiovascular defects in klf2a or klf2b single mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–P) which can survive to become fertile adults.
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–P

claim: klf2a transcript levels are significantly reduced in klf2abns11 mutants compared to their WT siblings
source: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis of klf2a, klf2b and klf4a mRNA levels shows that klf2a transcript levels are significantly reduced in klf2abns11 mutants compared to their WT siblings, suggesting nonsense-mediated decay.
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2Q

claim: klf2b mRNA levels are increased in klf2abns11 mutants compared to their WT siblings
source: In addition, the levels of klf2b and klf4a mRNA are increased in klf2abns11 mutants compared to their WT siblings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2Q), indicating that they could be compensating for the loss of Klf2a function.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2Q

claim: klf4a mRNA levels are increased in klf2abns11 mutants compared to their WT siblings
source: In addition, the levels of klf2b and klf4a mRNA are increased in klf2abns11 mutants compared to their WT siblings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2Q), indicating that they could be compensating for the loss of Klf2a function.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2Q

claim: klf2a and klf4a mRNA levels are increased in klf2bbns12 mutants compared to their WT siblings
source: Similarly, klf2a and klf4a mRNA levels are increased in klf2bbns12 mutants compared to their WT siblings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2R).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2R

claim: Most klf2 double mutants exhibit pericardial edema by 96 hours post fertilization
source: Unlike the single mutants, most double mutants exhibit pericardial edema by 96 hours post fertilization (hpf) (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by brightfield images in Figure 1C–D and quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: Abnormal atrioventricular canal elongation was observed at 48 hpf in approximately 10% of klf2 mutants
source: Abnormal atrioventricular (AV) canal elongation was observed at 48 hpf in approximately 10% of klf2 mutants (3/26).
evidence: Supported by quantitative observation of 3 out of 26 mutants

claim: AV valve formation was impaired in approximately 50% of klf2 mutants by 80 hpf
source: By 80 hpf, AV valve formation was clearly impaired in approximately 50% of klf2 mutants (17/36) as the canal appeared more elongated than in WT, and the multi-layering process leading to leaflet formation was also compromised in these animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–E), consistent with previous observations in klf2a morphants (Vermot et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–E, quantitative observation (17/36), and citation to Vermot et al., 2009

claim: The vascular network appeared unaffected in klf2 mutants
source: Although the vascular network appeared unaffected in klf2 mutants, most of them died by 2 weeks post-fertilization and none survived to adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by confocal images of vascular network in Figure 1—figure supplement 3F–H

claim: Most klf2 mutants died by 2 weeks post-fertilization
source: Although the vascular network appeared unaffected in klf2 mutants, most of them died by 2 weeks post-fertilization and none survived to adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3H

claim: None of the klf2 mutants survived to adulthood
source: Although the vascular network appeared unaffected in klf2 mutants, most of them died by 2 weeks post-fertilization and none survived to adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F–H).
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3H

claim: Approximately 90% of klf2 mutants exhibit cardiomyocyte extrusion toward the abluminal side at 96 hpf
source: Upon closer examination of their hearts at 96 hpf, we found that approximately 90% of klf2 mutants exhibit a previously unreported phenotype of cardiomyocyte extrusion toward the abluminal side (69/75 mutant hearts) (Figure 1E–J).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 1E–J and quantitative observation (69/75)

claim: The cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype first appears around 82 hpf in approximately 15% of klf2 mutants
source: This phenotype first appears around 82 hpf in approximately 15% of klf2 mutants (11/67 mutant hearts), and the number of extruding cardiomyocytes, which are mostly located in the outer curvature of the ventricle, is variable and increases over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B

claim: Extruding cardiomyocytes are mostly located in the outer curvature of the ventricle
source: This phenotype first appears around 82 hpf in approximately 15% of klf2 mutants (11/67 mutant hearts), and the number of extruding cardiomyocytes, which are mostly located in the outer curvature of the ventricle, is variable and increases over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B

claim: The number of extruding cardiomyocytes increases over time in klf2 mutants
source: This phenotype first appears around 82 hpf in approximately 15% of klf2 mutants (11/67 mutant hearts), and the number of extruding cardiomyocytes, which are mostly located in the outer curvature of the ventricle, is variable and increases over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B

claim: The size of klf2 mutant cardiomyocytes was significantly affected starting at 96 hpf
source: We also found that the size and circularity of klf2 mutant cardiomyocytes was significantly affected starting at 96 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–D)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–D

claim: The circularity of klf2 mutant cardiomyocytes was significantly affected starting at 96 hpf
source: We also found that the size and circularity of klf2 mutant cardiomyocytes was significantly affected starting at 96 hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–D)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C–D

claim: Around 60 percent of klf2 mutants exhibit impaired cardiac contractility at 96 hpf
source: We found that around 60 percent of klf2 mutants exhibit impaired cardiac contractility at 96 hpf.
evidence: Supported by observational data

claim: Impaired contractility induced by amhc or tnnt2a morpholinos does not induce cardiomyocyte extrusion in WT animals
source: We observed that impaired contractility could not induce cardiomyocyte extrusion in WT animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that this phenotype is not secondary to impaired contractility.
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Injecting tnnt2a MOs into klf2 mutants at the one-cell stage blocked cardiomyocyte extrusion
source: However, injecting tnnt2a MOs into klf2 mutants at the one-cell stage blocked cardiomyocyte extrusion (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 2A

claim: Short-term inhibition of cardiac contractility by BDM treatment from 100 to 102 hpf blocked cardiomyocyte extrusion
source: In addition, short-term inhibition of cardiac contractility by BDM treatment from 100 to 102 hpf could also block cardiomyocyte extrusion (4/5 hearts) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse confocal images in Figure 2B and quantitative observation (4/5 hearts)

claim: Cardiac contractility is required for cardiomyocyte extrusion in klf2 mutants
source: Overall, these data indicate that cardiac contractility is required for cardiomyocyte extrusion in klf2 mutants, and that this extrusion is reversible.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that blocking contractility prevents extrusion

claim: Cardiomyocyte extrusion in klf2 mutants is reversible
source: Overall, these data indicate that cardiac contractility is required for cardiomyocyte extrusion in klf2 mutants, and that this extrusion is reversible.
evidence: Inferred from BDM treatment data showing extruding cells returning to compact layer

claim: Extruding cardiomyocytes in klf2 mutants do not appear to be dying
source: In order to investigate the cause of the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype in klf2 mutants, we first performed Acridine Orange staining and found that the extruding cardiomyocytes in klf2 mutants did not appear to be dying (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by Acridine Orange staining images in Figure 3A–D

claim: The rate of atrial cardiomyocyte proliferation appeared unchanged in klf2 mutants compared to their WT siblings
source: we used the Tg(myl7:mVenus-gmnn) line (Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016; Uribe et al., 2018) which allows one to visualize actively proliferating cardiomyocytes in green, and found that while the rate of atrial cardiomyocyte proliferation appeared unchanged in klf2 mutants compared to their WT siblings, the levels of ventricular cardiomyocyte proliferation were considerably reduced (Figure 3E–I)
evidence: Supported by confocal images and quantification in Figure 3E–I, and citations to Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016 and Uribe et al., 2018

claim: The levels of ventricular cardiomyocyte proliferation were considerably reduced in klf2 mutants
source: we used the Tg(myl7:mVenus-gmnn) line (Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016; Uribe et al., 2018) which allows one to visualize actively proliferating cardiomyocytes in green, and found that while the rate of atrial cardiomyocyte proliferation appeared unchanged in klf2 mutants compared to their WT siblings, the levels of ventricular cardiomyocyte proliferation were considerably reduced (Figure 3E–I)
evidence: Supported by confocal images and quantification in Figure 3E–I, and citations to Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016 and Uribe et al., 2018

claim: Crowding is not the cause of the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype in klf2 mutants
source: we used the Tg(myl7:mVenus-gmnn) line (Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016; Uribe et al., 2018) which allows one to visualize actively proliferating cardiomyocytes in green, and found that while the rate of atrial cardiomyocyte proliferation appeared unchanged in klf2 mutants compared to their WT siblings, the levels of ventricular cardiomyocyte proliferation were considerably reduced (Figure 3E–I), suggesting that crowding is not the cause of the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype in klf2 mutants.
evidence: Inferred from reduced proliferation data

claim: Inhibition of cardiomyocyte proliferation in zebrafish can reduce the total number of cardiomyocytes while not leading to their extrusion
source: These observations are consistent with recent reports that inhibition of cardiomyocyte proliferation in zebrafish can reduce the total number of cardiomyocytes while not leading to their extrusion (Liu et al., 2010; Uribe et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2010 and Uribe et al., 2018

claim: N-cadherin is highly enriched in mouse and zebrafish cardiomyocytes
source: It has been reported that N-cadherin (Cdh2), an adhesion molecule, is highly enriched in mouse and zebrafish cardiomyocytes (Kostetskii et al., 2001; Bagatto et al., 2006; Cherian et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kostetskii et al., 2001, Bagatto et al., 2006, and Cherian et al., 2016

claim: Cdh2-EGFP molecules are highly enriched on the lateral sides of WT cardiomyocytes at 96 hpf
source: We thus examined the distribution of Cdh2-EGFP molecules using the TgBAC(cdh2:cdh2-EGFP) line (Revenu et al., 2014), and found that while they are highly enriched on the lateral sides of WT cardiomyocytes at 96 hpf, they have become mislocalized from the lateral to the apical side of cardiomyocytes in klf2 mutants (Figure 3J–M')
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 3J–M' and citation to Revenu et al., 2014

claim: Cdh2-EGFP molecules have become mislocalized from the lateral to the apical side of cardiomyocytes in klf2 mutants
source: We thus examined the distribution of Cdh2-EGFP molecules using the TgBAC(cdh2:cdh2-EGFP) line (Revenu et al., 2014), and found that while they are highly enriched on the lateral sides of WT cardiomyocytes at 96 hpf, they have become mislocalized from the lateral to the apical side of cardiomyocytes in klf2 mutants (Figure 3J–M'), suggesting that cardiomyocyte adhesion is affected.
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 3J–M' and citation to Revenu et al., 2014

claim: Knockdown of N-cadherin by injecting cdh2 MO at the one-cell stage can cause a cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype in WT hearts
source: In addition, knockdown of N-cadherin by injecting cdh2 MO at the one-cell stage can also cause a cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype in WT hearts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Cardiomyocyte extrusion correlates with the mislocalization of N-cadherin on their membranes
source: Overall, these data suggest that cardiomyocyte extrusion correlates with the mislocalization of N-cadherin on their membranes but not with cardiomyocyte cell death or proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing N-cadherin mislocalization in extruding cells

claim: Cardiomyocyte extrusion does not correlate with cardiomyocyte cell death
source: Overall, these data suggest that cardiomyocyte extrusion correlates with the mislocalization of N-cadherin on their membranes but not with cardiomyocyte cell death or proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from Acridine Orange staining showing no cell death

claim: Cardiomyocyte extrusion does not correlate with cardiomyocyte proliferation
source: Overall, these data suggest that cardiomyocyte extrusion correlates with the mislocalization of N-cadherin on their membranes but not with cardiomyocyte cell death or proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from proliferation data showing reduced proliferation in mutants

claim: Cardiomyocytes in the compact layer are polarized in their apicobasal axis
source: It has recently been shown that cardiomyocytes in the compact layer are polarized in their apicobasal axis whereas during the trabeculation process, they lose this polarity as they delaminate (Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016

claim: During the trabeculation process, cardiomyocytes lose their apicobasal polarity as they delaminate
source: It has recently been shown that cardiomyocytes in the compact layer are polarized in their apicobasal axis whereas during the trabeculation process, they lose this polarity as they delaminate (Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiménez-Amilburu et al., 2016

claim: At 96 hpf, extruding cardiomyocytes do not lose their apical polarity
source: In order to further investigate the extruding cardiomyocytes, we checked their apicobasal polarity by generating a myocardial-specific apical transgenic line, Tg(−0.2myl7:tdtomato-podxl), in which the apical protein podocalyxin is fused with tdTomato, and found that at 96 hpf, extruding cardiomyocytes do not lose their apical polarity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: There was no significant difference in terms of cardiac jelly thickness between klf2 WT and mutant animals at 96 hpf
source: Utilizing high-resolution confocal microscopy at 96 hpf, we observed that there was no significant difference in terms of cardiac jelly thickness between klf2 WT and mutant animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: At 55 hpf, a few tcf21-positive cells attach to the abluminal side of the ventricle
source: At 55 hpf, we observed a few tcf21-positive cells attaching to the abluminal side of the ventricle, which was fully covered by 96 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–H), in agreement with previous studies (Virágh and Challice, 1981; Peralta et al., 2013; Peralta et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–H and citations to Virágh and Challice, 1981, Peralta et al., 2013, Peralta et al., 2014, and Wang et al., 2015

claim: The ventricle was fully covered by tcf21-positive cells by 96 hpf
source: At 55 hpf, we observed a few tcf21-positive cells attaching to the abluminal side of the ventricle, which was fully covered by 96 hpf (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–H), in agreement with previous studies (Virágh and Challice, 1981; Peralta et al., 2013; Peralta et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A–H and citations to Virágh and Challice, 1981, Peralta et al., 2013, Peralta et al., 2014, and Wang et al., 2015

claim: At 96 hpf, there are fewer tcf21-positive cells covering the klf2 mutant hearts compared to their WT siblings
source: At 96 hpf, we observed fewer tcf21-positive cells covering the klf2 mutant hearts compared to their WT siblings, and also a sparser distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 4I–M), suggesting defective epicardial-myocardial interactions in the absence of Klf2 function.
evidence: Supported by confocal images and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 4I–M

claim: Epicardial ablation using metronidazole treatment from 48 to 96 hpf can induce cardiomyocyte extrusion
source: We found that this epicardial ablation approach could also induce cardiomyocyte extrusion; however, the number of extruding cardiomyocytes after epicardial ablation was far lower than that observed in klf2 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 4N–R).
evidence: Supported by confocal images and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 4N–R

claim: The number of extruding cardiomyocytes after epicardial ablation was far lower than that observed in klf2 mutants
source: We found that this epicardial ablation approach could also induce cardiomyocyte extrusion; however, the number of extruding cardiomyocytes after epicardial ablation was far lower than that observed in klf2 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 4N–R).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 4N–R

claim: WT donor-derived cardiomyocytes extrude from klf2-/- but not klf2+/? hearts
source: We first transplanted Tg(myl7:MKATE-CAAX) WT cells into Tg(myl7:LIFEACT-GFP); klf2+/?or klf2-/- hosts. Using confocal microscopy, we found that at 96 hpf some WT donor-derived cardiomyocytes were extruding from klf2-/- but not klf2+/? hearts (Figure 4A–E; n = 7 hearts).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 4A–E and quantitative observation (n = 7 hearts)

claim: klf2-/- cardiomyocytes do not extrude when transplanted into WT hosts
source: We also performed the converse experiment by transplanting Tg(myl7:LIFEACT-GFP); klf2+/?or klf2-/- cells into WT hosts and observed no extruding klf2-/- cardiomyocytes (Figure 4F–J; n = 9 hearts).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 4F–J and quantitative observation (n = 9 hearts)

claim: Klf2 function is not required in cardiomyocytes to maintain the integrity of the myocardial wall
source: These data indicate that Klf2 function is not required in cardiomyocytes to maintain the integrity of the myocardial wall.
evidence: Inferred from cell transplantation experiments showing WT cardiomyocytes extrude in mutant hearts but mutant cardiomyocytes do not extrude in WT hearts

claim: In zebrafish, klf2 is expressed in the endocardium
source: In zebrafish, as in mouse, klf2 is expressed in the endocardium (Lee et al., 2006; Vermot et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2006 and Vermot et al., 2009

claim: klf2b becomes expressed in the zebrafish heart by 36 hpf
source: Similar to klf2a, klf2b also becomes expressed in the zebrafish heart by 36 hpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization images in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Myocardial klf2a and klf2b overexpression caused pericardial edema in about forty percent of the F1 and F2 animals when observed at 96 hpf
source: Unlike endothelial klf2b overexpression, myocardial klf2a and klf2b overexpression caused pericardial edema and impaired trabeculation in about forty percent of the F1 and F2 animals when observed at 96 hpf.
evidence: Supported by observational data

claim: Myocardial klf2a and klf2b overexpression caused impaired trabeculation in about forty percent of the F1 and F2 animals when observed at 96 hpf
source: Unlike endothelial klf2b overexpression, myocardial klf2a and klf2b overexpression caused pericardial edema and impaired trabeculation in about forty percent of the F1 and F2 animals when observed at 96 hpf.
evidence: Supported by observational data

claim: Cardiac defects from myocardial klf2 overexpression became milder beyond the F2 generation
source: These cardiac defects became milder beyond the F2 generation.
evidence: Supported by observational data

claim: Endothelial klf2b overexpression rescued the pericardial edema observed in klf2 mutant hearts
source: Notably, we observed that endothelial, but not myocardial, klf2b overexpression rescued the pericardial edema as well as the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutant hearts (Figure 5A–P), indicating the importance of endothelial/endocardial klf2 expression in maintaining myocardial wall integrity.
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 5A–P

claim: Endothelial klf2b overexpression rescued the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutant hearts
source: Notably, we observed that endothelial, but not myocardial, klf2b overexpression rescued the pericardial edema as well as the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutant hearts (Figure 5A–P), indicating the importance of endothelial/endocardial klf2 expression in maintaining myocardial wall integrity.
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 5A–P

claim: Myocardial klf2b overexpression did not rescue the pericardial edema observed in klf2 mutant hearts
source: Notably, we observed that endothelial, but not myocardial, klf2b overexpression rescued the pericardial edema as well as the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutant hearts (Figure 5A–P)
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 5A–P

claim: Myocardial klf2b overexpression did not rescue the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutant hearts
source: Notably, we observed that endothelial, but not myocardial, klf2b overexpression rescued the pericardial edema as well as the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutant hearts (Figure 5A–P)
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 5A–P

claim: Endothelial klf2b overexpression rescued the reduction of ventricular cardiomyocyte proliferation observed in klf2 mutants
source: We also quantified the number of proliferative cardiomyocytes in klf2 WT and mutant animals overexpressing klf2b in their endothelium and found that the reduction of ventricular cardiomyocyte proliferation observed in klf2 mutants was rescued by endothelial klf2b overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by confocal images and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Endothelial klf2b overexpression rescued the epicardial defects observed in klf2 mutants
source: Interestingly, endothelial klf2b overexpression also rescued the epicardial defects observed in klf2 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by confocal images and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: Endothelial/endocardial klf2 is required for myocardial wall integrity by regulating endocardial-myocardial-epicardial interactions
source: Overall, these data indicate that endothelial/endocardial klf2 is required for myocardial wall integrity by regulating endocardial-myocardial-epicardial interactions.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing endothelial klf2b overexpression rescues multiple phenotypes

claim: Endothelial rescue approach rescued almost sixty percent of klf2 mutant larvae to become adults
source: Although all klf2 mutant larvae die, we were able to rescue almost sixty percent of them to become adults using this endothelial rescue approach (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by images and survival data in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–B

claim: No significant differences were observed between klf2 WT and rescued mutant adult hearts
source: Dissecting the adult hearts, we did not observe any significant differences between klf2 WT and rescued mutant hearts, further suggesting the importance of endothelial klf2 expression in maintaining myocardial wall integrity (Figure 5Q–R' and Figure 5—figure supplement 4C–F).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 5Q–R' and Figure 5—figure supplement 4C–F

claim: aldh1a2 is up-regulated in klf2 mutant hearts
source: Our transcriptome data show that aldh1a2 and cyp26b1, the highest expressing cyp26 gene in 96 hpf hearts, are respectively up- and down-regulated in klf2 mutant hearts (Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting an increase in retinoic acid (RA) levels.
evidence: Supported by microarray data in Figure 6—source data 1

claim: cyp26b1 is down-regulated in klf2 mutant hearts
source: Our transcriptome data show that aldh1a2 and cyp26b1, the highest expressing cyp26 gene in 96 hpf hearts, are respectively up- and down-regulated in klf2 mutant hearts (Figure 6—source data 1), suggesting an increase in retinoic acid (RA) levels.
evidence: Supported by microarray data in Figure 6—source data 1

claim: Excess levels of RA in cyp26a1 and cyp26c1 morphants lead to the failure of second heart field progenitors to join the outflow tract
source: It has recently been reported that excess levels of RA in cyp26a1 and cyp26c1 morphants lead to the failure of second heart field progenitors to join the outflow tract as well as the extrusion of first heart field-derived cardiomyocytes from the ventricle at 48 hpf (Rydeen and Waxman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rydeen and Waxman, 2016

claim: Excess levels of RA in cyp26a1 and cyp26c1 morphants lead to the extrusion of first heart field-derived cardiomyocytes from the ventricle at 48 hpf
source: It has recently been reported that excess levels of RA in cyp26a1 and cyp26c1 morphants lead to the failure of second heart field progenitors to join the outflow tract as well as the extrusion of first heart field-derived cardiomyocytes from the ventricle at 48 hpf (Rydeen and Waxman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rydeen and Waxman, 2016

claim: RA treatment from 74 to 96 hpf did not cause cardiomyocyte extrusion in WT zebrafish larvae
source: In order to test whether increased RA signaling causes cardiomyocyte extrusion at later stages, we treated WT zebrafish larvae with RA from 74 to 96 hpf but did not observe any extruding cardiomyocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Hedgehog signaling was downregulated in klf2 mutant hearts
source: We also found that Hedgehog (Hh) signaling was downregulated in klf2 mutant hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2 and Figure 6—source data 2)
evidence: Supported by GSEA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2

claim: Inhibition of Hh signaling in WT zebrafish from 75 to 96 hpf using Cyclopamine did not cause cardiomyocyte extrusion
source: however, inhibition of this pathway in WT zebrafish from 75 to 96 hpf using Cyclopamine, a Hh signaling pathway inhibitor, did not cause cardiomyocyte extrusion (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 6—figure supplement 3

claim: By itself increased RA signaling does not cause the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutants
source: Together, these data indicate that by itself increased RA signaling or inhibition of Hh signaling does not cause the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutants.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing RA treatment and Hh inhibition do not cause extrusion

claim: By itself inhibition of Hh signaling does not cause the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutants
source: Together, these data indicate that by itself increased RA signaling or inhibition of Hh signaling does not cause the cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype observed in klf2 mutants.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing RA treatment and Hh inhibition do not cause extrusion

claim: Fgf signaling has been implicated in the formation of the compact myocardial layer
source: Fgf signaling has been implicated in the formation of the compact myocardial layer as well as in cardiomyocyte differentiation and proliferation (Reifers et al., 2000; Lavine et al., 2005; Marques et al., 2008; Tirosh-Finkel et al., 2010; Pradhan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reifers et al., 2000, Lavine et al., 2005, Marques et al., 2008, Tirosh-Finkel et al., 2010, and Pradhan et al., 2017

claim: Fgf signaling has been implicated in cardiomyocyte differentiation
source: Fgf signaling has been implicated in the formation of the compact myocardial layer as well as in cardiomyocyte differentiation and proliferation (Reifers et al., 2000; Lavine et al., 2005; Marques et al., 2008; Tirosh-Finkel et al., 2010; Pradhan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reifers et al., 2000, Lavine et al., 2005, Marques et al., 2008, Tirosh-Finkel et al., 2010, and Pradhan et al., 2017

claim: Fgf signaling has been implicated in cardiomyocyte proliferation
source: Fgf signaling has been implicated in the formation of the compact myocardial layer as well as in cardiomyocyte differentiation and proliferation (Reifers et al., 2000; Lavine et al., 2005; Marques et al., 2008; Tirosh-Finkel et al., 2010; Pradhan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reifers et al., 2000, Lavine et al., 2005, Marques et al., 2008, Tirosh-Finkel et al., 2010, and Pradhan et al., 2017

claim: Fgf signaling is affected in klf2 mutants
source: Transcriptomic analysis of klf2 WT and mutant hearts shows that Fgf signaling is affected in klf2 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Figure 6—source data 3 and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: Supported by GSEA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and gene expression data in Figure 6—source data 3

claim: Several fgf receptor and ligand genes are expressed at reduced levels in klf2 mutant compared to WT hearts
source: follow up qPCR analysis shows that several fgf receptor and ligand genes are expressed at reduced levels in klf2 mutant compared to WT hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 4

claim: Treatment with SU5402 from 75 to 96 hpf caused cardiomyocyte extrusion in 7 out of 9 hearts
source: To test the role of Fgf signaling in myocardial wall integrity, we treated Tg(myl7:EGFP-Has.HRAS) larvae from 75 to 96 hpf with SU5402, a FGF receptor inhibitor, and observed cardiomyocyte extrusion (7/9 hearts; Figure 6A–D)
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 6A–D and quantitative observation (7/9 hearts)

claim: Treatment with SU5402 from 75 to 96 hpf caused mislocalization of Cdh2-EGFP from the lateral to the apical side of cardiomyocytes in 10 out of 11 hearts
source: as well as mislocalization of Cdh2-EGFP from the lateral to the apical side of cardiomyocytes (10/11 hearts; Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 6—figure supplement 5 and quantitative observation (10/11 hearts)

claim: Global overexpression of dominant negative Fgfr1 caused cardiomyocyte extrusion in 9 out of 13 hearts
source: In addition, global overexpression of dominant negative Fgfr1, using the Tg(hsp70:dn-fgfr1-EGFP) line (Lee et al., 2005), could also cause cardiomyocyte extrusion (9/13 hearts; Figure 6E–H)
evidence: Supported by confocal images in Figure 6E–H, quantitative observation (9/13 hearts), and citation to Lee et al., 2005

claim: The number of extruding cardiomyocytes in animals overexpressing dominant negative Fgfr1 was less than that observed in klf2 mutants or SU5402 treated animals
source: however, the number of extruding cardiomyocytes in these animals was less than that observed in klf2 mutants or SU5402 treated animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 6—figure supplement 6A

claim: The cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype appeared in only a few SU5402 treated hearts by 82 hpf
source: While, this cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype appeared in only a few SU5402 treated hearts by 82 hpf (7/36 hearts), the number of extruding cardiomyocytes increased over time, as in klf2 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 6—figure supplement 6B–D and quantitative observation (7/36 hearts)

claim: The number of extruding cardiomyocytes in SU5402 treated animals increased over time
source: While, this cardiomyocyte extrusion phenotype appeared in only a few SU5402 treated hearts by 82 hpf (7/36 hearts), the number of extruding cardiomyocytes increased over time, as in klf2 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 6B–D).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 6—figure supplement 6B–D

claim: Inhibition of Fgfr signaling can cause cardiomyocyte extrusion
source: These data indicate that inhibition of Fgfr signaling can cause cardiomyocyte extrusion, as in klf2 mutants.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing SU5402 treatment and dnfgfr1 overexpression cause extrusion

claim: klf2a+/-; klf2b-/- animals were more sensitive to Fgfr signaling inhibition compared to WT
source: We also treated WT and klf2a+/-; klf2b-/- larvae with DMSO or increasing concentrations of SU5402 and found that klf2a+/-; klf2b-/- animals were more sensitive to Fgfr signaling inhibition, that is more prone to exhibit cardiomyocyte extrusion compared to WT (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 6I

claim: Fgfr inhibition reduced pERK immunostaining
source: We further treated WT larvae with SU5402 from 75 to 96 hpf and then stained their hearts with a pERK antibody. Our data show that Fgfr inhibition reduced pERK immunostaining (Figure 6—figure supplement 7), in agreement with previous reports (Shinya et al., 2001; Calmont et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images in Figure 6—figure supplement 7 and citations to Shinya et al., 2001 and Calmont et al., 2006

claim: dnfgfr1 overexpression reduced pERK immunostaining, although milder than that observed in SU5402-treated hearts
source: We also checked pERK immunostaining after dnfgfr1 overexpression and observed a reduction, although milder than that observed in SU5402-treated hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images in Figure 6—figure supplement 7

claim: pERK immunostaining was significantly reduced in endocardial cells of klf2 mutants compared to WT
source: We further found that pERK immunostaining was significantly reduced in endocardial cells of klf2 mutants compared to WT (Figure 6J and K)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images in Figure 6J and K

claim: pERK immunostaining in klf2 mutants was rescued by endothelial klf2b overexpression
source: and that it was rescued by endothelial klf2b overexpression (Figure 6L and M).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images in Figure 6L and M

claim: Fgf signaling is required downstream of Klf2 to maintain myocardial wall integrity
source: Overall, these data suggest that Fgf signaling is required downstream of Klf2 to maintain myocardial wall integrity.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing Fgfr inhibition causes extrusion and pERK is reduced in klf2 mutants

claim: Most fgf receptor genes are expressed in the zebrafish heart
source: By examining single-cell RNA sequencing data of early zebrafish embryos (https://kleintools.hms.harvard.edu/paper_websites/wagner_zebrafish_timecourse2018/mainpage.html; Wagner et al., 2018), we found that most fgf receptor genes and many fgf ligand genes are expressed in the zebrafish heart (Figure 6—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data in Figure 6—figure supplement 8 and citation to Wagner et al., 2018

claim: Many fgf ligand genes are expressed in the zebrafish heart
source: By examining single-cell RNA sequencing data of early zebrafish embryos (https://kleintools.hms.harvard.edu/paper_websites/wagner_zebrafish_timecourse2018/mainpage.html; Wagner et al., 2018), we found that most fgf receptor genes and many fgf ligand genes are expressed in the zebrafish heart (Figure 6—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data in Figure 6—figure supplement 8 and citation to Wagner et al., 2018

claim: myl7 expression levels were unaffected in npas4l mutant hearts compared to WT
source: As expected, myl7 expression levels were unaffected in npas4l mutant hearts compared to WT while fli1a levels were significantly reduced (Figure 6—figure supplement 9A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 9A

claim: fli1a expression levels were significantly reduced in npas4l mutant hearts compared to WT
source: As expected, myl7 expression levels were unaffected in npas4l mutant hearts compared to WT while fli1a levels were significantly reduced (Figure 6—figure supplement 9A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 9A

claim: Expression levels of all fgf receptor genes were slightly increased in npas4l mutants
source: Expression levels of all fgf receptor genes were slightly increased in npas4l mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 9B), suggesting that they are not expressed in the endocardium.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 9B

claim: fgf14 expression was reduced in npas4l mutant hearts
source: Analyzing Fgf ligand genes which are clearly downregulated in klf2 mutants, we observed a reduction in fgf14 expression in npas4l mutant hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 9C), suggesting its endocardial enrichment.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 9C

claim: fgf3 expression was upregulated in npas4l mutant hearts
source: We also observed an upregulation of fgf3 expression in npas4l mutant hearts (Figure 6—figure supplement 9C), suggesting that it is not expressed in the endocardium.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 9C

claim: Genes associated with adherens junctions are affected in klf2 mutants
source: Transcriptomic analysis of klf2 WT and mutant hearts also indicates that genes associated with adherens junctions and focal adhesions are affected in klf2 mutants, further suggesting the importance of Klf2 in myocardial wall integrity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Genes associated with focal adhesions are affected in klf2 mutants
source: Transcriptomic analysis of klf2 WT and mutant hearts also indicates that genes associated with adherens junctions and focal adhesions are affected in klf2 mutants, further suggesting the importance of Klf2 in myocardial wall integrity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Endocardial klf2 regulates myocardial wall integrity at least in part by modulating myocardial Fgfr signaling
source: Overall, our data suggest that endocardial klf2 regulates myocardial wall integrity at least in part by modulating myocardial Fgfr signaling.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing Fgfr inhibition causes extrusion and klf2 affects Fgf signaling

claim: Klf2 -/- mice die between E12.5 and E14.5 due to hemorrhaging and cardiovascular failure
source: Klf2 -/- mice die between E12.5 and E14.5 due to hemorrhaging and cardiovascular failure (Lee et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2006 and Wu et al., 2008

claim: A noticeable reduction in ventricular wall thickness was observed in global and endothelial-specific Klf2 mouse mutants
source: A noticeable reduction in ventricular wall thickness was observed in global and endothelial-specific Klf2 mouse mutants, albeit no significant changes in cardiomyocyte proliferation or death were reported (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2006

claim: No significant changes in cardiomyocyte proliferation or death were reported in Klf2 mouse mutants
source: A noticeable reduction in ventricular wall thickness was observed in global and endothelial-specific Klf2 mouse mutants, albeit no significant changes in cardiomyocyte proliferation or death were reported (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2006

claim: KLF2 loss-of-function enhances endothelial leakage in HUVECs upon thrombin treatment
source: KLF2 has also been implicated in maintaining endothelial barrier integrity, as KLF2 loss- or gain-of-function respectively enhances or prevents endothelial leakage in HUVECs upon thrombin treatment (Lin et al., 2010).

claim: KLF2 gain-of-function prevents endothelial leakage in HUVECs upon thrombin treatment
source: KLF2 has also been implicated in maintaining endothelial barrier integrity, as KLF2 loss- or gain-of-function respectively enhances or prevents endothelial leakage in HUVECs upon thrombin treatment (Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin et al., 2010

claim: Detachment of the epicardium from the myocardial surface was reported in Klf2 mutant hearts in mouse
source: Detachment of the epicardium from the myocardial surface was also reported in Klf2 mutant hearts in mouse (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2006

claim: Inhibition of Fgf signaling in mouse embryos by mosaic overexpression of Sprouty2 causes a cell-shedding phenotype in the hepatic epithelium
source: Interestingly, it has been reported that inhibition of Fgf signaling in mouse embryos, by mosaic overexpression of Sprouty2, causes a cell-shedding phenotype in the hepatic epithelium (Calmont et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Calmont et al., 2006

claim: Fgf signaling can have cardioprotective effects by modulating the phosphorylation of the gap junction protein connexin 43
source: Fgf signaling can have cardioprotective effects by modulating the phosphorylation of the gap junction protein connexin 43 (Srisakuldee et al., 2006), which itself can interact with N-cadherin in cell-cell adhesion (Wei et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Srisakuldee et al., 2006 and Wei et al., 2005

claim: Connexin 43 can interact with N-cadherin in cell-cell adhesion
source: Fgf signaling can have cardioprotective effects by modulating the phosphorylation of the gap junction protein connexin 43 (Srisakuldee et al., 2006), which itself can interact with N-cadherin in cell-cell adhesion (Wei et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wei et al., 2005

claim: cdon is downregulated in klf2 mutant hearts
source: Interestingly, we also found a downregulation in klf2 mutant hearts of cdon, which is highly expressed in early zebrafish hearts based on single-cell sequencing data (Wagner et al., 2018) and encodes a cell adhesion molecule implicated in myoblast and neuronal differentiation via binding to N-cadherin (Lu and Krauss, 2010)
evidence: Supported by transcriptome data and citations to Wagner et al., 2018 and Lu and Krauss, 2010

source: Interestingly, we also found a downregulation in klf2 mutant hearts of cdon, which is highly expressed in early zebrafish hearts based on single-cell sequencing data (Wagner et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wagner et al., 2018

claim: Cdon encodes a cell adhesion molecule implicated in myoblast and neuronal differentiation via binding to N-cadherin
source: Interestingly, we also found a downregulation in klf2 mutant hearts of cdon, which is highly expressed in early zebrafish hearts based on single-cell sequencing data (Wagner et al., 2018) and encodes a cell adhesion molecule implicated in myoblast and neuronal differentiation via binding to N-cadherin (Lu and Krauss, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu and Krauss, 2010

claim: Cdon-mediated N-cadherin localization has been reported to be crucial in neural crest cell migration
source: Cdon-mediated N-cadherin localization has also been reported to be crucial in neural crest cell migration (Powell et al., 2015).

claim: Cdon expression is induced by KLF2 in vitro
source: Cdon expression is induced by KLF2 in vitro (Boon, 2008).

claim: egr1 is a flow responsive transcription factor gene involved in FGF-dependent angiogenesis during neo-vascularization and tumor growth
source: We further found that egr1, a flow responsive transcription factor gene involved in FGF-dependent angiogenesis during neo-vascularization and tumor growth (Khachigian et al., 1997; Khachigian, 2006), is downregulated in klf2 mutant hearts.
evidence: Supported by citations to Khachigian et al., 1997 and Khachigian, 2006

claim: Both Klf2 and Fgf signaling are required to maintain myocardial wall integrity
source: Altogether, our data suggest that both Klf2 and Fgf signaling are required to maintain myocardial wall integrity
